subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: In photosynthesis, light energy is converted into:
choices: Chemical energy in carbon compounds
Heat energy released to the air
Kinetic energy of water molecules
Electrical energy in the chloroplast
items.note: Light is transformed into chemical energy stored in glucose and other organic molecules.

items.stem: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from:
choices: Carbon dioxide
Glucose
Chlorophyll
Water
items.note: Photolysis splits water; the O₂ is a waste product. Isotope experiments with ¹⁸O confirmed this.

choices: Absorbs green light most strongly
Emits green light when its electrons are excited
Reflects green light and absorbs red and blue
Absorbs all wavelengths of light equally
items.note: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue; green is reflected or transmitted.

choices: The amount of light absorbed by each separate pigment
The rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength of light
The concentration of each pigment in a leaf
The wavelengths of light reaching the leaf
items.note: Absorption spectrum = light absorbed per wavelength; action spectrum = photosynthesis rate per wavelength. They match closely.

items.stem: In paper chromatography of leaf pigments, the Rf value is:
choices: Distance moved by the solvent ÷ distance moved by the pigment
Distance moved by the pigment ÷ distance moved by the solvent
Distance moved by the pigment × distance moved by the solvent
Distance from the origin to the bottom of the paper
items.note: Rf = pigment distance ÷ solvent front distance, always between 0 and 1.

items.stem: At high light intensity, increasing the CO₂ concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis. This shows that:
choices: CO₂ concentration was the limiting factor
Light intensity was the limiting factor at that point
Temperature was the limiting factor
No factor was limiting the rate
items.note: The factor in shortest supply limits the rate. If raising CO₂ raises the rate, CO₂ was limiting.

items.stem: Growers add CO₂ to glasshouses mainly to:
choices: Reduce the temperature inside the glasshouse
Kill insect pests that feed on the crop plants
Increase the water uptake by the roots
Increase the rate of photosynthesis and so the yield
items.note: CO₂ enrichment raises the rate when CO₂ is limiting, increasing growth, as long as light and temperature are not limiting.

items.stem: In the light-dependent reactions, photolysis of water:
choices: Produces the CO₂ that is fixed in the Calvin cycle
Supplies the energy that drives ATP synthase directly
Replaces the electrons lost by photosystem II
Reduces NADP using electrons from photosystem I
items.note: Excited electrons leave PS II; water splitting provides replacement electrons, plus protons and O₂.

items.stem: In the Calvin cycle, the enzyme Rubisco catalyses:
choices: The reduction of glycerate 3-phosphate to triose phosphate
The regeneration of RuBP using ATP
The splitting of water in the thylakoid lumen
The fixation of CO₂ onto ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP)
items.note: Rubisco joins CO₂ to RuBP (5C), forming two glycerate 3-phosphate (3C) molecules.

items.stem: ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent reactions are used in the Calvin cycle to:
choices: Fix carbon dioxide onto RuBP using Rubisco
Convert glycerate 3-phosphate into triose phosphate
Split water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen
Pump protons into the thylakoid space
items.note: GP is reduced to triose phosphate using NADPH and ATP. ATP is also used to regenerate RuBP.

items.stem: If a plant in light is suddenly put in darkness, the concentration of RuBP in the chloroplast:
choices: Falls, because ATP and NADPH are no longer made to regenerate it
Rises, because CO₂ fixation continues faster in the dark
Stays constant, because the Calvin cycle does not need light
Rises, because photolysis of water stops producing oxygen
items.note: Without light, no ATP/NADPH, so GP cannot be converted to TP and RuBP is not regenerated, while fixation still uses RuBP up.

items.stem: Explain how temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis.
markscheme: Rate increases with temperature up to an optimum (1)
Because enzymes (e.g. Rubisco) and molecules move faster, more collisions (1)
Above the optimum, enzymes denature, so rate falls (1)
items.tactic: Same shape as an enzyme curve: name the enzyme-controlled stage.

items.stem: Outline how leaf pigments can be separated by chromatography.
markscheme: Grind leaf with solvent/sand to extract pigments; spot a concentrated sample on a pencil origin line (1)
Place in solvent with the origin above the solvent level (1)
Pigments move different distances due to different solubility/attraction to paper; calculate Rf values (1)
items.tactic: Practical outlines: preparation, running, and how results are interpreted.

items.stem: Explain how ATP is produced by chemiosmosis in the chloroplast.
markscheme: Excited electrons pass along the electron transport chain in the thylakoid membrane (1)
Energy is used to pump protons into the thylakoid space (1)
A proton gradient forms across the thylakoid membrane (1)
Protons diffuse back through ATP synthase into the stroma (1)
This drives phosphorylation of ADP to ATP (photophosphorylation) (1)
items.tactic: Trace the energy: light → electrons → proton gradient → ATP synthase.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Oxygen bubbles per minute from an aquatic plant at different light intensities (arbitrary units) and two CO₂ concentrations: low CO₂ — 10: 8, 20: 15, 40: 22, 60: 23, 80: 23; high CO₂ — 10: 8, 20: 16, 40: 30, 60: 41, 80: 44.
(a) Identify the limiting factor at light intensity 10, with evidence. (b) Identify the limiting factor at light intensity 80 for low CO₂, with evidence. (c) Explain why bubble counting may underestimate the rate.
markscheme: (a) Light intensity: both CO₂ levels give the same rate (8) at intensity 10 (1)
(b) CO₂ concentration: rate levels off at 23 for low CO₂ but is higher (44) with high CO₂ (1)
(c) Bubbles vary in size / some O₂ dissolves in water or is used in respiration (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
